method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report' (published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275)), 24 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11343900). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024) 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey' (published 6 March 2025), 8 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12077586). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Source text: Europe PMC fullTextXML of the Diabetologia co-publication (CC BY 4.0). The Diabetes Care version (PMC11272983) is under a non-alteration licence and its full text was not available through Europe PMC or NCBI efetch, so it was not used. Edition 2.0 keeps every Edition 1.0 claim (S1) unchanged and adds S2, a 2024 national survey of DKA protocols at 31 Australian hospitals (Intern Med J 2025; CC BY-NC-ND, so paraphrased and hash-anchored), for the Australian angle. S2 is a practice survey, not a guideline, and gives no diagnostic pH or bicarbonate cut-offs.

claims.claim: **DKA needs all three: hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), raised ketones and metabolic acidosis.** The glucose threshold has been lowered to 11.1 mmol/L, and a person with known diabetes qualifies at any glucose level.
claims.source_text: The diagnosis of DKA should be based on the three criteria described in Fig. 2a. All three components must be present to make this diagnosis. In this consensus report, we have defined hyperglycaemia as a diagnostic criterion for DKA from >13.9 mmol/l (250 mg/dl) to either a glucose value of ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) or a prior history of diabetes irrespective of the presenting glucose value.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **About 10% of DKA is euglycaemic (glucose below 11.1 mmol/L).** Causes include SGLT2 inhibitors (now the majority of cases), reduced food intake, pregnancy, alcohol and liver failure.
claims.source_text: Approximately 10% of patients with DKA present with euglycaemic DKA, which is defined as plasma glucose levels <11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) in the presence of ketosis and metabolic acidosis criteria of DKA described in Fig. 2 [, ]. Euglycaemic DKA can be caused by a variety of factors, including exogenous insulin injection, reduced food intake, pregnancy, or impaired gluconeogenesis due to alcohol use, liver failure and/or SGLT2 inhibitor therapy [, ]. In recent years, the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in those with type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes has accounted for the majority of cases of euglycaemic DKA
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure blood β-hydroxybutyrate (venous or capillary) to diagnose and to monitor treatment**, not urine nitroprusside ketones. A level of 3.0 mmol/L or more has over 90% sensitivity and specificity for DKA.
claims.source_text: Thus, for diagnosis and monitoring of the response to therapy, we recommend direct measurement of venous or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate, which is the main ketoacid in DKA [, ]. Blood concentrations of β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/l correlate well with acid-base changes, with >90% sensitivity and specificity
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First tests:** glucose, electrolytes, venous blood gas, full blood count and ketones. Examine for infection, ischaemia and other precipitants, and do an ECG (hyperkalaemia, ischaemia).
claims.source_text: If DKA or HHS is suspected, initial samples should be taken for glucose, serum electrolytes, venous blood gases, complete blood count, and blood or urine ketone levels. … Patients should be examined for signs of infection, ischaemia and other potential precipitants of a hyperglycaemic crisis. In addition, an electrocardiogram should be performed to assess for evidence of biochemically induced repolarisation abnormalities, such as peaked T waves from hyperkalaemia and ischaemia.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for the trigger:** infection is the commonest worldwide (14–58% of cases), and missed insulin is a major cause. Glucocorticoids, antipsychotics and immune checkpoint inhibitors can also precipitate a crisis.
claims.source_text: Worldwide, infection is the most common precipitating factor for DKA, occurring in 14-58% of cases … The omission of insulin therapy, often in the setting of psychological and socioeconomic factors, is a major cause of DKA … Some drug classes can affect carbohydrate metabolism and precipitate the development of DKA and HHS []. Glucocorticoids may precipitate acute and sustained hyperglycaemia by countering insulin action [, ]. Antipsychotic medications may also raise DKA risk, although the precise mechanism is uncertain []. Approximately 1-2% of patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors develop new-onset autoimmune diabetes [], characterised by rapid onset of hyperglycaemia, swift progression of endogenous insulin deficiency, and a high risk of DKA or severe hyperglycaemia if not detected and treated promptly with insulin therapy
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other causes of ketosis to exclude:** starvation ketosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis, and ketosis of pregnancy or hyperemesis.
claims.source_text: It is important to consider the differential diagnosis of elevated ketones, including starvation ketosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis, and ketosis of pregnancy and hyperemesis
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Abdominal pain may be caused by DKA or may be its trigger.** Re-examine if it does not settle once dehydration and acidosis have been corrected.
claims.source_text: Caution is needed with patients who present with abdominal pain because the symptoms could be either a result of the DKA or an indication of a precipitating cause of DKA, particularly in the absence of severe metabolic acidosis. Further clinical evaluation is necessary if this complaint is not resolved with the resolution of dehydration and metabolic acidosis.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA can be managed in the emergency department or a step-down unit** with close nursing monitoring. Severe DKA, HHS, a critical-illness trigger or altered mental state belongs in ICU.
claims.source_text: Most people with uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA can be treated in the emergency department or a step-down unit if close nursing supervision and monitoring are available … In contrast, individuals with severe DKA or HHS, or those with critical illness as the precipitating cause (e.g., myocardial infarction, gastrointestinal bleeding, sepsis) or with altered mental status [, ] should be treated in the ICU
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Capillary glucose every 1–2 h; bloods every 4 h** (electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, β-hydroxybutyrate, venous pH) until DKA resolves.
claims.source_text: Capillary blood glucose testing should be performed during treatment every 1-2 h using a hospital-calibrated glucose meter, and blood should be drawn every 4 h for determination of electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, β-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH until resolution of DKA.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500–1000 ml/h for the first 2–4 h** if there is no renal or cardiac compromise, and correct the estimated deficit over 24–48 h. Balanced crystalloids resolved DKA faster than saline in recent studies.
claims.source_text: In adults with DKA or HHS without renal or cardiac compromise, we recommend starting the administration of isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid solutions at an initial rate of 500-1000 ml/h during the first 2-4 h. … Fluid replacement should correct estimated deficits within the first 24-48 h. … Recent prospective and observational studies and meta-analyses have reported that the administration of balanced crystalloid solutions (e.g., Ringer's lactate or plasmalyte-148), compared with the administration of the isotonic saline solution, results in faster DKA resolution
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Older adults, heart failure and dialysis patients:** use smaller boluses (e.g. 250 ml) and reassess haemodynamics often.
claims.source_text: Older adults with DKA or HHS, as well as individuals with heart failure or end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, should be treated cautiously with smaller boluses of isotonic or crystalloid solutions (e.g., 250 ml boluses) and should undergo frequent assessment of haemodynamic status
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start insulin as soon as possible after diagnosis: intravenous short-acting insulin by fixed-rate infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h** (or a nurse-driven variable-rate protocol). Give a 0.1 U/kg bolus IV or IM only if venous access will be delayed.
claims.source_text: Insulin therapy is the cornerstone of DKA management and should be started as soon as possible after diagnosis. Short-acting insulin administered intravenously by continuous infusion is the preferred choice. Depending on the severity of the condition and the available facilities, this should be done using a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion started at 0.1 U kg-1 h-1 [-, ] or by a nurse-driven insulin infusion protocol with a variable rate for DKA … In adults, treatment protocols recommend the initial administration of an insulin bolus (0.1 U/kg) (intravenously or intramuscularly) if a delay in obtaining venous access is anticipated to be followed by fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **When glucose falls below 13.9 mmol/L, add 5–10% dextrose and halve insulin to 0.05 U/kg/h**, aiming for glucose around 11.1 mmol/L. Keep the insulin running until the ketoacidosis has resolved.
claims.source_text: Once the blood glucose falls below 13.9 mmol/l (250 mg/dl), 5-10% dextrose should be added to the 0.9% saline infusion and the insulin infusion rate should be reduced to 0.05 U kg-1 h-1. Thereafter, intravenous insulin infusion should be adjusted to maintain glucose levels at approximately 11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) and continued until the ketoacidosis is resolved
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Continue the patient's usual basal insulin.** Adding low-dose basal insulin (0.15–0.3 U/kg) during the infusion shortened time to resolution and hospital stay without more hypoglycaemia.
claims.source_text: In people on basal or basal-bolus insulin therapy before admission, this regimen can be continued at the usual dose and adjusted as needed. … Several studies have reported that the coadministration of a low dose (0.15-0.3 U/kg) of basal insulin during insulin infusion reduces time to DKA resolution, duration of insulin infusion [, ] and length of hospital stay [] and prevents rebound hyperglycaemia, all without increased risk
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild or moderate uncomplicated DKA can be treated with subcutaneous rapid-acting analogue every 1–2 h** instead of an infusion. Do not use this for severe or complicated DKA or for HHS.
claims.source_text: Several randomised studies and a meta-analysis have reported that the administration of subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues every 1-2 h is an effective alternative to intravenous infusion of short-acting insulin for people with mild or moderate DKA … The use of rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin analogues is not recommended for the treatment of severe and complicated DKA or with HHS.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Potassium: once below 5.0 mmol/L, replace to keep 4–5 mmol/L; 20–30 mmol per litre of fluid is usually enough.** If potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L at presentation, give 10 mmol/h and **hold insulin until it is above 3.5 mmol/L**.
claims.source_text: To prevent hypokalaemia, potassium replacement should be started after serum levels fall below 5.0 mmol/l to maintain a potassium level of 4-5 mmol/l [, ]. For most patients with DKA, 20-30 mmol of potassium per litre of intravenous fluid is sufficient to maintain a serum potassium concentration within the target range. Low-normal or low potassium levels (<3.5 mmol/l) are present on admission in 5-10% of patients with DKA []; in such cases, potassium replacement should begin at a rate of 10 mmol/h, and insulin therapy should be delayed until the potassium level increases to >3.5 mmol/l to avoid life-threatening arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check potassium 2 h after insulin starts and then every 4 h** until DKA resolves.
claims.source_text: To avoid hypokalaemia, we recommend measuring serum potassium 2 h after starting insulin administration and every 4 h thereafter until the resolution of DKA.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No routine bicarbonate.** Consider it only if pH is below 7.0: 100 mmol sodium bicarbonate (8.4%) in 400 ml sterile water every 2 h until pH is above 7.0.
claims.source_text: Routine bicarbonate administration is not recommended. … bicarbonate administration should be considered if the acidosis is severe (i.e., pH <7.0) [, ]. If indicated, then 100 mmol of sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) in 400 ml of sterile water (an isotonic solution) can be given every 2 h to achieve a pH >7.0
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No routine phosphate.** Replace only with muscle weakness, or respiratory or cardiac compromise, and phosphate below 1.0 mmol/L; 20–30 mmol potassium phosphate can go into the fluids.
claims.source_text: unless there is evidence of muscle weakness, such as respiratory or cardiac compromise with the phosphate <1.0 mmol/l, routine administration of phosphate is not indicated. … When necessary, 20-30 mmol of potassium phosphate can be added to replacement fluids.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **DKA has resolved when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is 7.3 or more (or bicarbonate 18 mmol/L or more)**, ideally with glucose below 11.1 mmol/L. Do not use the anion gap or urine ketones to judge resolution.
claims.source_text: Resolution of DKA is defined as achieving plasma ketone <0.6 mmol/l and venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/l []. Ideally, the blood glucose concentration should also be <11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl). The anion gap should not be used as a criterion, as it may be misleading because of the presence of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis caused by large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride solution. Because β-hydroxybutyrate is converted into acetoacetate as the acidosis improves, urinary ketone measurement should be avoided as a criterion of DKA resolution.
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Overlap subcutaneous and IV insulin by 1–2 h.** For insulin-naive patients estimate a total daily dose of 0.5–0.6 U/kg/day, or about 0.3 U/kg/day with frailty or kidney failure. If baseline therapy was inadequate or a drug contributed, change the regimen before discharge.
claims.source_text: it is important to allow an overlap of 1-2 h between the administration of subcutaneous insulin and the discontinuation of intravenous insulin. … First, a weight-based formula may be considered for TDD calculation using 0.5-0.6 U kg-1 day-1 in insulin-naive patients, with the understanding that body composition and/or insulin resistance may have an impact on this estimate [, ]. Similarly, for people with risk factors for hypoglycaemia, including kidney failure or frailty, a calculation using approximately 0.3 U kg-1 day-1 may be more appropriate. … If there is concern for inadequate baseline insulin therapy (i.e., high HbA1c) or any potentially precipitating drug as a contributing factor to the DKA or HHS event, then the treatment regimen should be changed at discharge and not deferred to outpatient follow-up
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **HHS insulin: fixed-rate 0.05 U/kg/h without significant ketonaemia or acidosis; 0.1 U/kg/h if it is mixed DKA/HHS.** Glucose should fall by no more than 5–6.7 mmol/L per hour, and sodium by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h.
claims.source_text: If HHS is present with no ketosis or with mild or moderate ketonaemia (blood β-hydroxybutyrate ≥1.0 to <3.0 mmol/l or urine ketones <2+) and without acidosis (pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/l), then a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion should be started at 0.05 U kg-1 h-1. If significant ketonaemia is present (i.e., β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/l, ketonuria ≥2+, pH <7.30 or bicarbonate <18 mmol/l), which represents mixed DKA/HHS, then a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion should be started at 0.1 U kg … the decline should not exceed 5-6.7 mmol l-1 h-1 (90-120 mg dl-1 h-1) to prevent cerebral oedema. Similarly, the rate of decline of serum sodium should not exceed 10 mmol/l in 24 h
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Before discharge:** education on the episode and on diabetes self-management, sick-day advice, an insulin supply, and ketone testing. Offer CGM after discharge and follow up within 2–4 weeks.
claims.source_text: Before discharge, all individuals admitted with DKA or HHS should be offered appropriate education focused on both the current event and overall diabetes management. … close follow-up within 2-4 weeks after discharge may reduce recurrent DKA … real-time or intermittently scanned CGM should be offered to people admitted with DKA after hospital discharge
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Screen everyone with a hyperglycaemic crisis for mental health problems** (for example PHQ-9 for depression). Suicide-attempt risk is highest in the 12 months after DKA.
claims.source_text: with the highest risk of suicide attempt in the 12 months following the DKA episode … all individuals experiencing hyperglycaemic crises should be screened for mental health concerns. The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) is the most used and validated screening test for depression
claims.locator: American Diabetes Association, European Association for the Study of Diabetes, Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, American Association of Clinical Endocrinology and Diabetes Technology Society (Umpierrez GE et al.), Diabetologia, 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', published 22 June 2024 (co-published in Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Insulin infusions differ across Australia:** in a national survey covering 31 hospitals, 39% of DKA protocols used a fixed rate, 45% a variable (glucose-titrated) rate and 16% a mix, and the responding clinicians were evenly divided in which they preferred.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **What the fixed or mixed protocols used:** nearly all set the rate by weight, most often 0.1 and/or 0.05 u/kg (one used 0.07 u/kg; one used a flat 4 u/h). Only 10% started with an IV insulin bolus (all variable-rate protocols), and 68% said to keep giving subcutaneous basal insulin.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Where DKA is managed in Australia varies:** mainly the emergency department in 29% of hospitals, ICU in 26%, a high-dependency unit in 13% and the ward in 32%; 77% had written criteria for ICU admission.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Most Australian protocols still name 0.9% sodium chloride** (86% of those naming a fluid; only three chose a balanced crystalloid) and 70% of clinicians prefer it, for reasons such as premixed potassium bags, familiarity and cost, and a view that hyperchloraemia matters little beside ketosis.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **SGLT2-inhibitor ketoacidosis is under-addressed:** 55% of protocols mentioned SGLT2 inhibitors but only 16% managed it differently. Because it runs closer to normal glucose, a variable-rate infusion may under-treat it unless extra dextrose is given early, and a fixed-rate infusion needs added dextrose to prevent hypoglycaemia.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Resolution criteria, where written (67% of protocols), are close to S1's:** most used pH above 7.3 (two used above 7.35), and 77% used ketones below 0.6 mmol/L, with the rest ranging from below 0.3 to below 1.0 mmol/L.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The S2 authors dispute the international push for fixed-rate infusions:** no regimen has been shown superior, and fixed rates bring more hypoglycaemia (28% in a 2014 UK audit, after which UK guidance added halving from 0.1 to 0.05 u/kg/h once glucose is below 14 mmol/L). Variable rates usually give about 2.6–3.5 u/h, against 7 u/h for a 70-kg adult on a weight-based protocol. Until better evidence exists they would support both, chosen by local capacity with a focus on avoiding hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.
claims.locator: Raven LM, Lever W, MacIsaac RJ, Greenfield JR, Deane A, et al., Internal Medicine Journal 55(5):728-733 (doi 10.1111/imj.70024), 'Heterogeneity in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in Australia: a national survey', published 6 March 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12077586/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2 calls for an Australian national consensus,** starting with how DKA is diagnosed and when it has resolved, so outcomes of the different infusion regimens can be compared.
